newsitem.title: UK: Britain hopes for U.S. help on N.Ireland ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Britain hopes for U.S. help on N.Ireland ceasefire.

text.p: Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam set off for Washington on Thursday in search of U.S. pressure for an IRA ceasefire.
In her first trip abroad since the Labour Party's landslide May 1 election victory, Mowlam will hold two days of talks with members of Congress and senior members of the U.S. administration.

The new government has sought to breathe new life into the peace process this week by ordering the first talks between British officials and Sinn Fein since its military wing, the IRA, ended a ceasefire in February 1996.

"I shall encourage those Americans with Northern Ireland's best interests at heart -- and there are many of them -- to bring their influence to bear on Sinn Fein to respond to the prime minister's initiative, seeking a restoration of an unequivocal ceasefire that would enable Sinn Fein to enter the talks process," she said in a statement.

"Until Sinn Fein are able to grasp the political reality of this fact they will not be able to take up their seats on the settlement train which, as the prime minister stressed on his visit to Belfast last week, will be leaving whether they are on it or not."
President Bill Clinton last week welcomed Blair's overtures to Sinn Fein as "a balanced and constructive step towards restoring momentum to the peace process".

Mowlam's visit, during which she is expected to meet Senator Edward Kennedy and National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, comes less than two weeks before the resumption of multi-party peace talks on Northern Ireland, which are chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell.
Sinn Fein will not be allowed to join the talks until the IRA calls a credible ceasefire. Mowlam has said she does not expect Sinn Fein to be present when the talks resume on June 3 in Belfast.

Mowlam described the search for peace in Northern Ireland, gripped by three decades of sectarian and political conflict that has killed more than 3,000 people, as one of the most challenging jobs for any minister.
Mowlam said she remained optimistic and would underline the Labour government's commitment to seeking a peaceful settlement acceptable to all sections of the community in Northern Ireland.

But the new minister has already run into trouble with one vocal section of that community as a Protestant politician accused her of siding with Irish nationalists by saying London would press ahead with talks even if the Protestants walked out.

"She has been giving the impression since she arrived in Northern Ireland that she is favouring the (Roman Catholic) nationalist community," declared Democratic Unionist Party deputy chief Peter Robinson.
"She has taken leave of her senses," thundered his leader Ian Paisley.

Britain's efforts to set up all-party talks, involving Sinn Fein and Unionist groups, were stymied last year by the Irish Republican Army's decision to end a 17-month ceasefire and resume a bombing and shooting war aimed at ending rule from London.
Mowlam said she would also use her U.S. visit to encourage further U.S. investment in Northern Ireland.
